en: An Explanation of the Chapter on Śūraṅgama-vīrya’s Perfect Penetration from the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, composed by Qing Xingce.

This single scripture, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, is said to have been taught after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; it is truly the inner sanctum of the Buddha-dharma. Formerly, the Dharma Master Zhizhe...

At the time of the classification of teachings (panjiao), this sutra had not yet reached China; therefore, only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* were regarded as the "final flavor" (the *tīruma*).
Had they been seen at that time, there would certainly have been extensive commentaries and exegeses, and it would undoubtedly have been classified as the *tīruma*.

Alas, the Great Beings who are the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*) have already passed away, and the masters of commentaries throughout past and present have each promoted divergent views. For a long time, these have been like a public dispute, leaving later students without the means to discern the truth.
Regarding the Dharma-eye, there is no fixed path to follow. To desire to completely discard commentaries and exegeses and look only at the scriptural text is itself an overly extreme argument.
Furthermore, when one uses one's own intellect to seek out the scriptures, one often fails to grasp their essential meaning, resulting ultimately in nothing but obscurity.
Let us try to judge with an impartial mind: how could the various interpretations lack merit? Yet, they do not fall into the error of contradiction.
This is erroneous; it is immediately lost in its oversimplification. Occasionally, there are those of superior intelligence who transcend their peers;

they then take this sutra as a means to manifest what lies within their own minds. If they can establish theories that possess truth, setting aside their own views to follow the sutra and bending to accord with the Buddha’s intent, then—with the exception of Master Jian’s *Shu* (Commentary) on the West Lake—I have not seen anyone else capable of matching such beauty. Who would say that people of the present age must necessarily...?
Can one not surpass the ancients? Some may find his advocacy excessive, and it is not without reason that they criticize him for fabricating doctrines.

Even if there are indeed some regrets, he has nonetheless rendered great service to this sutra. As for the teaching that abandons consciousness (*vijñāna*) to employ the sense faculties (*indriya*), placing primary emphasis on the doctrine of perfect penetration—this is the sincere word of the Buddhas;
who would dare not believe it? Regarding the essence of the teachings in this land... who [would doubt it]?
I dare not fail to comply with this. Those who debate against it are all those who contravene the scriptures and oppose the Buddha.
It is truly rare to find present-day virtuous friends who have already set their minds upon the Pure Land and further wish to study this sutra.

Nevertheless, setting aside its beginning and end for a moment, there are many points of confusion and error within this very section on "Perfect Penetration. Unless one is skilled at reading and skillful at interpreting it, then—
The so-called "ghee" and "poisonous medicine" are not far apart.
Have you not heard that at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the field for selecting Buddhas was opened, where Avalokiteśvara passed the examination while Śākyamuni (Śrī-garbha) failed?

If those who cultivate the Pure Land do not discern this distinction here, how can they realize the secret intent of this sūtra and strengthen the practice and vows of future students? It is only the dharma-gate of Śākyamuni...

This is not the essential meaning of this sutra; therefore, even Master Jian cited it in his commentary but did not elaborate upon it. Here, I shall first distinguish the dharma-gate and subsequently reveal its esoteric intent.
Regarding the distinction of the dharma-gate:
one should know that this holy, perfect penetration belongs to the element of "root" among the seven elements, as it universally encompasses the other six.
Because of the faculties (*indriya*). Based on these six faculties, one cultivates the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).

There are three types of distinctions: first, recollecting one's own Buddha; second, recollecting another Buddha; and third, recollecting both one's own and another Buddha. If one recollects one's own Buddha, this is identical to the perfect penetration of all the Sages.
This takes the nature of the faculties as the dharma-gate that is recollected, and taking the revolving of the tranquil essence as the means of recollection.

It is appropriate. As stated in the *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra*: "That is to say, regarding the faculty of the eye, he constantly cultivates it in full perfection without diminution for all Tathāgatas, seeing with perfect clarity;
and so on, up to: regarding the faculty of the mind, he constantly cultivates it in full perfection without diminution for all Tathāgatas, knowing with perfect clarity.
This is also as in this sūtra, where the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively address Ānanda, commanding him...
You shall swiftly realize the blissful liberation of wondrous, eternal quiescence. These six faculties of yours are nothing other than this.
As the Patriarch said: "In the womb it is called the body; dwelling in the world it is called a person; in the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing."
Discerning fragrance with the nose, engaging in discourse with the mouth, grasping with the hands, and running about with the feet—the wise know these to be Buddha-nature;
those who do not recognize them call them the vital spirit (*sūkṣma-ātman*). The various patriarchs of the past have pointed this out in many such ways.
This mindfulness itself encompasses all doctrinal meanings through the samādhi of the Buddhas; it is the direct pointing dharma-gate of all Chan schools, leaving nothing unexhausted.

It is not exhaustive. If one contemplates another Buddha, it differs from the perfect penetration of the various sages. This is because the six sense faculties serve as the subject of contemplation, while the resultant Buddha serves as the object of contemplation.
Although the Dharma-body is of one essence, I lack the two kinds of adornment, whereas the Buddhas possess the perfection of merit and wisdom, becoming the Honored Ones of Two Feet.
Contemplating those resultant virtues, one never gives rise to weariness; the eyes constantly gaze [upon them].
The Buddha’s marks: the ears constantly hear the Buddha’s teachings; the nose constantly perceives the Buddha’s fragrance; the tongue constantly recites the Buddha’s name;

the body constantly prostrates before the Buddha’s image; and the mind constantly takes the Buddha’s Dharma as its object. That which the six sense organs attend to is nothing other than the realm of the Buddha. Thus, these states succeed one another without interruption or confusion.
This is the Samādhi of Mindfulness of Another Buddha, which fully encompasses all [the Buddhas], such as Amitābha, Bhaiṣajyaguru, and Maitreya.
This includes the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and other scriptures, as well as all the practices and contemplative methods of the Lotus Society, leaving nothing unexhausted.

If one contemplates the Buddhas of oneself and others, one will achieve perfect penetration with the various sages; yet, while being identical, there is also a distinction. First, one must open up a sudden and perfect understanding.

To realize that the birth of a Buddha and one’s own mind are of one suchness, and that the land and the mind are non-dual; to rely upon those environments and beings to manifest one's own mind-nature;

and thus, being no longer deluded regarding anything external to this nature, neither to cling to the existence of a Buddha nor to hold that the land is not the mind—this is the point where one opens the perfect understanding shared with all the sages.
To rely upon the objective realm of others is what distinguishes one from the sages. This is what the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* calls the "superior and extraordinary skillful means."

The present text states that one need not rely on expedient means to attain the opening of the mind spontaneously; because this expedient is supreme and exceptionally distinct, no further expedients are required.

Within the context of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiao*), I shall briefly distinguish the great function of gathering in and transforming sentient beings through the three types of Buddha-remembrance samādhis (*nianfo sanmei*) in relation to the four kinds of pure lands.
As for those who contemplate only their own Buddha, they are gathered back into the serene land of true recompense (*shibao jijing*).

Although this illuminates the two types of pure lands, it can only allow for vertical entry and not horizontal transcendence; furthermore, it only accommodates those of sharp faculties and cannot universally encompass all practitioners;

moreover, since this is common to all sages, it does not manifest the unique distinction of this specific gate. Thus, it seems not to accord with the essential intent of Śrī-Ābhāsvara’s inclusion [of beings].

Now, I maintain that it correctly encompasses two types of practitioners: those who practice mindfulness of another Buddha, and those who practice mindfulness of both themselves and another Buddha. It brings them back [to the ultimate goal].
Within the Land of Common Abode, one simultaneously and transversely transcends the lands of Expedient Means, True Reward, and Peaceful Light;
therefore, the text deeply clarifies the benefit of the mutual resonance between the response of the Buddha and the invocation of the practitioner.
Next, to reveal the underlying intent (*saṃdhi*) of the sūtra: the selection of the dharma-gate of perfect penetration is like a state employing troops and selecting its generals.
Some are promoted to lead as vanguard; others are pressed into service to bring up the rear.

Those brought up the rear are the primary selections, while the rest merely follow their respective regular units. These promotions and pressings do not occur without cause; it is just as with the eighteen [armies].
Within the realms (*dhātu*), the standard order is invariably that the sense organs (*indriya*) come first, followed by the objects (*viṣaya*), and finally consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Now, however, the six objects are placed first and the organs second; furthermore, among the six objects, color-form (*rūpa*) normally precedes sound (*śabda*), followed by odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
Now, sound is placed at the very beginning and color-form second. Moreover, among the six organs, only five are listed here, having extracted the ear organ (*śrotrendriya*) and placed it [elsewhere].

Following the twenty-four gates, it is because the essence of the True Teaching of this land lies in the purity of sound within hearing that sound-objects are presented first and the faculty of hearing is placed last, and thus it alone is explained in detail.
Although the reason for this is not explicitly stated, people have already perceived it.
Having centered the emphasis on the gateway of the ear, the essential points of this sutra are arranged as the application of the Dharma of Perfect Penetration.

It is so. Nevertheless, the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*) is also suited to the capacities of those in this land. Sentient beings in the final age must rely upon Buddha-remembrance to attain liberation;

thus, this sutra causes one to enter deeply through a single gate and directly realize one's own nature (*svabhāva*). If one were to instead select both gates simultaneously, one would obscure the essential purport of this sutra.
If it were to cause the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance to be practiced indiscriminately alongside the common ranks [of other practices], [the specific intent of this teaching would be lost].
Furthermore, this misses the intent of the extensive praise found in other sutras; therefore, it now skillfully demonstrates a hidden suppression.
Just as a secret military order is not permitted to be leaked, previously, within the eighteen *dhātus*, the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) was clearly identified as the principal general;

now, within the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*), the element of the faculties (*indriya-mahābhūta*) is implicitly suppressed as the principal general. And this element of the faculties properly belongs to the Buddha-remembrance practice (*nien-fo*).
This approach does not contradict the intent of other sutras that extensively praise [the elements], nor does it deviate from the meaning of this sutra’s application of the sense organs;
it may be called both supremely skillful and supremely subtle. As for the sequence of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), they are: earth, water, fire, wind, space, seeing, and consciousness.

Seeing is the fundamental faculty; logically, the faculty should come first and consciousness second. Now, consciousness has been moved to the sixth position, while the faculty is placed at the end of the "Great Palace" (the five sense organs).
This is also like the Ear-door among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, within the preceding five great elements, fire is promoted to the vanguard, followed by earth, water, wind, and space. This has two intentions: first, to suit the specific capacity of the audience.
Because the teaching was initiated by the occurrence of lust, it invokes fire through excessive lust to warn those of great learning to first eliminate the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
Thus the text says: "It is said that a person of much lust becomes a mass of fierce fire," and so on, until "transforming the mind of much lust into the fire of wisdom."
The Buddhas called me by the name Huotou (Fire-Head). By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I have attained Arhatship.
I vow to serve as a mighty warrior to personally subdue the demonic enemies and the like; this is to awaken them through clarity.
In all sūtras and vinayas, non-killing is universally regarded as the foremost precept; however, in this sūtra, celibacy is established as the primary and definitive instruction. Regarding...

Among the three conditions, the reason why lustful craving is placed before killing and stealing is precisely this same intent. Second, it serves as an antidote for the heavy obstacles of the末法 (mofa) age;
for although afflictions are many, only sexual desire is the root of birth and death, and is most capable of obstructing rebirth in the Dharma.
Thus, it causes the practitioner to contemplate that the fire of lust within the body of an ordinary person is, in its very nature, the Tathāgatagarbha—the true emptiness.
Fire manifests according to one's karma; through profound contemplation, one attains awakening and it becomes the light of wisdom.
It does not merely fail to obstruct rebirth, but can actually escort the practitioner to be entrusted to the highest grade of rebirth.

This is why the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* praises lust, anger, and ignorance, for their essence is identical to the *tathāgatagarbha*, and the shift between defilement and purity occurs with the flip of a hand. Thus, the fire-headed deity is placed at the forefront. Furthermore—
They were like the Dignāga among the eighteen *dhātus*. Now, let us examine the various sages:
setting aside these two vanguard generals and the two heavy-duty marshals, all others may be seen to follow the established precedent exactly, their sequence unerring.

When the twenty-five sages rose from their seats and when the great disciples performed the compilation (*saṃgīti*), their singular majesty and decorum, their single movement and single stillness, were consistent throughout.
All of these possess profound meaning and are entirely in accord with the principles of the teachings. How could one possibly grasp them with a coarse mind?

Nevertheless, although it may appear that Avalokiteśvara alone has passed the examination, how could it be that Śrī-vasa has failed altogether? It is simply that for Avalokiteśvara there is an explicit selection, whereas for Śrī-vasa there is an implicit selection.

This is truly because those with faculties of perfect integration enter separately, and thus there is an explicit selection; whereas since all marks are universally subsumed, [there is an implicit selection].

"Selection by Manifestation": Because this is the teaching-body (*śāsana-deha*) of this region, it is selected through manifestation. "Selection by Concealment": Because there are those with karmic affinity in this land, it is selected through concealment. "Manifest Selection":

Because it universally benefits sentient beings of the present and future who are present at the assembly of the occasion, it is selected through manifestation. "Concealed Selection": Because it specifically benefits sentient beings in the evil age of the Dharma’s end who do not see the Buddha, it is selected through concealment.
A tiger-banner placed high and manifest is known by all people; a crimson robe marked in secret is known only by those at the time.
They do not realize this; therefore, it is said that there is great confusion and error here. One must read and comprehend it skillfully. Someone may ask:

"If this is a secret meaning (*samdhāya-bhāṣita*), how can it be leaked? I reply: "The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* has been displayed as the banner of the field for selecting Buddhas for over two thousand years.
If its secrets were not clearly exposed and broken open at this time, what would be the use of such secrecy? Another may say: "If it is truly as you say, then Mañjuśrī spoke..."

When choosing [the verses] according to the gāthās, could one not also understand the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*)? Why not follow the previous precedent and select them all at once? [The response:

The various sages each spoke of their own "first" [realization] when they personally recounted their experiences; thus, by means of mutual comparison and suppression, they skillfully revealed the subtle mechanism [of the teaching].

If one were to strictly select according to the formal command, following the previous rules exactly, how could it constitute a "secret" [teaching]? Nevertheless, the element of fire (*tejas*) within the sense-object of sound (*śabda-dhātu*) is nonetheless categorized as permanent (*nitya*).
Next, these two gates are presented as auxiliary means to clarify specific points; they are not the primary focus of this work, and therefore will not be further elaborated upon.
As for the section on Śrī-Prabhūtaratna (Potu), it follows the prose narrative by being placed after the "Great Consciousness" (Vijñānadhātu) to serve as the finale of the twenty-four gates.
There has never been one who did not follow this principle. Furthermore, since you have already instructed that a single school be selected exclusively, how could you fail to choose Śrīmatī?
Examining her words of selection, they still differ from those of the other sages; she merely says: "The causes and effects are now distinct; how can one attain perfect penetration?"

The meaning is this: although those [practitioners] fully encompass the six sense faculties and maintain a succession of pure mindfulness, this successive mindfulness belongs to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) and is subject to flux;
it is, therefore, a phenomenon of arising and ceasing. To take this as the cause while desiring to be reborn to see the Buddha—who could say it is impossible?

However, if one now wishes to realize the non-arising and non-ceasing perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-prativedha*) in the present life, then cause and effect do not correspond; how then could such a result be attained? This...
The selection is made based on attaining perfect penetration in the present life; it does not pertain to the benefits obtained after rebirth.

As for the other sages who contemplate their own buddha-nature alone, they belong exclusively to the category of present cultivation and present realization. Therefore, they are entirely excluded, as they do not accord with the spiritual capacities and needs of the beings in this land.
This is because it does not accord with the essential substance of the teachings of this land. Those who are resolved to practice for realization should also reflect upon this deeply and at length.

However, this is spoken for those whose power of faith is not yet firm. If one possesses deep faith in the Pure Land, then even if the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* were to single out Aśvaghosha (Śrīmitra) for censure, one would still harbor no doubt. Why is this? Because other sutras praise him extensively. Thus it is said: "It is inconceivable."
When discussing its merits, it is described as a teaching difficult for the world to believe; as that which is protected by all Buddhas;

as the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna; as the supreme and extraordinary skillful means; and as the king among samādhis. Though praised extensively in many places, people still do not give rise to faith.
To suddenly blink at one point—how can you allow such doubt to arise? Moreover, it was never intended as a solitary disparagement, nor did it provide a covert selection [of one path over another].

Alas, those sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age who read this sutra are unable to follow the teachings to enter deeply through the ear-door and realize perfect penetration (*yuantong*) through direct manifestation;
instead, they are prone to harbor doubts regarding the Buddha-remembrance (*nianfo*) dharma-gate, even to the point of destroying the pure faith of others.
They obstruct the virtuous conduct of others; such is the habitual tendency of those with meager merit and little wisdom.
Therefore, I have here analyzed this matter in detail according to the Dharma and the scriptures, though I am not aware that my words have become so prolix. How could I help it?
Commentary on the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Śūraṅgama by Śvetāśva (End)
